slides.title: Sets

blocks.text: A set is a collection of elements with no duplicates.
Like the mathematical definition of a set.
The primary purpose is to determine whether a particular element is a member of a set.
Must have a fast way to lookup for an element in the set.
Other collections, such as lists, can also lookup an element.
However, it is more efficient to use sets for fast lookup.

The HashSet and TreeSet classes

blocks.text: HashSet and TreeSet are classes that implement Set
HashSet is implemented using the hashing technique
Elements are mapped and stored in a hash table
The HashSet class implements the hashCode method that computes and returns the hash value of a given object
The hashCode method is very efficient: time complexity is O(1)
TreeSet is implemented as a balanced binary search tree
The in-order traversal produces an ordered set of elements
The basic operations are implemented in O(log n) efficiency

slides.title: HashSet versus TreeSet

blocks.text: HashSet uses a hash table to implement a set
HashSet provides a faster lookup of elements
TreeSet uses a binary search tree, called Red-Black tree
TreeSet keeps the elements in order based on their values
Use HashSet when order of elements is not important but requires quick lookup of elements
Use TreeSet if the order of elements is important and there is frequent addition and removal of elements

slides.title: Maps

blocks.text: A map is an abstract data type that establishes an efficient mapping between keys and values.
A map stores key-value pairs (k, v), which are called entries.
The keys of a map must be unique.
Each key maps to only one value. However, multiple keys could map to the same value.
For example, a person id is used as a key mapped to a person object that contains name and address.

slides.title: Some Applications of Maps

blocks.text: Databases: fast lookup of data based on a key or index.
Caching: maps are used to save the results of database queries, such that subsequent requests can be served quickly.
Compilers: maps are used to implement symbol tables that map variable names to their corresponding memory location.
Web applications: maps are used to store session data and user login credentials for user authentication.
Language Models: fast retrieval of words and spell checkers.
Machine Learning: maps feature vectors to numeric values.

slides.title: The HashSet and HashMap Classes

blocks.text: The HashSet and HashMap classes are implemented using a technique called hashing.
The hashing technique uses a hash function to compute the location of an element in a hash table for fast access.
A function that maps each element to a unique location in a hash table is called a perfect hash function.
However, sometimes multiple elements are mapped to the same location in a hash table, which causes a collision.

slides.title: Hash Table

blocks.text: A hash table is an array of elements or map entries.
The hashing technique converts a key into an integer index.
Indexing an array is done is constant time = O(1)
The hash table array can be dynamically resized if the size of the data is not known in advance.
The main question is how large should the hash table be?
The load factor of a hash table is the percent of its full capacity.
For example, if the load factor is 0.75 then the hash table should be resized each time it reaches 75% of its full capacity.

slides.title: The Hashing Method in Java

blocks.text: The root class Object defines the hashCode method that returns an integer based on the object memory location.
Classes often override the hashCode method and provide their own version. For example, the String and Integer classes define their own version of hashCode.
It is also preferrable to define your own hashCode method for any object that you intend to store in a hash table.
If two objects are equal according to the equals() method, then their hashCode() values must also be the same.

slides.title: Overriding equals and hashCode

blocks.text: The implementation of the equals method describes what makes two instances of the class equal.
For example, two Course objects as equal if they have same prefix and number.
Typically, whenever the equals method is overridden, the hashCode method is also overridden.
Two equal objects must have the same hash code.
The inverse is not necessarily true: two unequal objects can have the same hash code.

slides.title: Collisions

blocks.text: If a hash table has N entries, then the hash code of a key is mapped to an index using the remainder operator:
index = Math.abs(key.hashCode() % N); // 0 to N-1
Collisions occur if two keys are mapped to the same index
The question is how to resolve collisions?
We can handle collisions using chaining. Rather than storing one entry at each index in a hash table, we can store a linked list of entries.
